notice: Historical assistant reports recovered from the original local prototype session. Reported measurements, not independently rerun. Proposals are not approvals. Later research corrects some conclusions; see ../jev-search-prototypes.md. Private transcript and tool inputs are not included.

reports.text:
The prototype now runs eight token-cut variants side by side and can retrieve fingerprint candidates from Qdrant. The typecheck is clean. I ran the pipeline for two requests, and the page rendered without errors in a temporary dev server. I haven't clicked through it in a browser.

## Why Crate was used so heavily

I chose Crate for the first version because it was quick to build. You're right that fingerprint retrieval belongs in Qdrant. The `fingerprint_v1` vector is the 74 raw scores in the same key order that the webapp uses. So Jev's dimension weights become the query vector, and the attribute decisions become payload filters.

Crate is still needed for two things that Qdrant doesn't hold:

- **Trope passages and full-text search:** Qdrant stores only trope names.
- **Synopsis, essence text, and tags:** One lookup by ID fetches these.

The page has a **Fingerprint retrieval** selector with three options. I compared the three options on two requests:

| Option | Speed | Candidates for "unreliable narrator" |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qdrant vector search | 0.4 s | Forgotten, Somebody to Love, Passengers, The Girl on the Train |
| Qdrant wide pool, re-ordered by weighted sum | 0.9 s | Stay, The Machinist, Shutter Island, Coherence, Anatomy of a Fall |
| Crate weighted sum | 0.7 s | Mulholland Drive, Mr. Robot, Perfect Blue, Westworld |

Plain Qdrant search is the fastest option, but its candidates look weaker. The collection uses cosine distance, which divides by the length of each title's vector. That favors titles with few strong scores, which are often obscure. The wide-pool option fetches 300 titles from Qdrant and re-orders them in code, which fixes most of that. Retrieval took longer for "tense but not bleak" (1.8 to 4.2 s), and Qdrant was faster than Crate there too.

## The variants

Every variant judges the same candidates, one variant after another, so each variant's time is measured directly. The **Search** columns show what one product search would cost: one request-reading call (14,278 tokens) plus that variant's fit calls. The numbers are from "unreliable narrator" with 36 candidates:

| Variant | Fit requests | Fit tokens | Search cost per 1,000 | Fit time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| No tropes | 36 | 37,291 | $2.17 | 1.2 s |
| Baseline with tropes | 36 | 44,844 | $2.48 | 0.9 s |
| No per-trope questions | 36 | 41,440 | $2.34 | 0.9 s |
| Lean title state | 36 | 35,569 | $2.09 | 0.8 s |
| Short fit levels | 36 | 42,684 | $2.39 | 0.9 s |
| Trope names only | 36 | 37,854 | $2.19 | 0.8 s |
| Batched, 8 titles per request | 5 | 33,136 | $1.99 | 0.5 s |
| All cuts combined | 5 | 21,701 | $1.51 | 0.3 s |

In that one search, the top 6 of every trope variant stayed inside the baseline's top 10. That's a single request, so don't treat it as a quality result.

## Reading the request

The page always runs the request-reading call twice, once with full level descriptions and once with short ones. It shows the two readings next to each other. The short version used 9,066 tokens and the full version used 14,278. For "unreliable narrator", the short version swapped `meta_narrative` for `pop_culture`, which looks like a worse reading. A selector sets which reading drives retrieval.

With the fit calls cut down, the request-reading call is now the largest single cost. It accounts for 14,000 of about 36,000 tokens in the "all cuts" search.

## Page changes

- Each result's details now include the exact title state that was sent to Jev for that variant.
- Rank changes are relative to the **Baseline with tropes** column.
- The columns show the top 12 results, with a toggle for all candidates.
- A search takes 10 to 20 seconds and costs about $0.013, because the page runs all eight variants.

The new comparison page is at `/prototype/jev-vector`. It runs five request-to-vector strategies one after another and shows speed, cost, and results per strategy. The typecheck is clean, and I ran three requests through the pipeline. I haven't opened the page in a browser.

On this page, Jev reads only the request. No title goes to Jev, and there are no fit calls or trope queries. The earlier page at `/prototype/jev-search` is unchanged, in case you want to return to it.

## The five strategies

| Strategy | How Jev reads the request | How the answer becomes a query |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A. Wanted level per dimension | 74 Score questions on a five-level ladder from avoid to central. This is the current approach. | The 8 strongest deviations from neutral become weights. |
| B. Want and avoid as yes/no | 148 Noul questions: does the request ask for the quality, and does it ask to avoid it. | The weight is the difference of the two probabilities. Every dimension above a threshold is used. |
| C. Ideal title profile | 74 Score questions on a ten-level ladder: how strongly would the ideal title express each quality. | The full 0 to 10 profile is the query vector, and Qdrant's cosine order is used as is. |
| D. Groups first, then dimensions | 5 Noul questions pick the relevant dimension groups. Then strategy A's Score runs only inside those groups. | Same as A. It needs two round trips. |
| E. Pick primary, secondary, avoided | 3 Choice questions over all 74 dimensions, each with a "none" option. | Weights are +2, +1, and -2, scaled by probability. |

Strategies A, B, D, and E fetch a pool of 300 titles from Qdrant, and code re-orders the pool by weighted sum. All five strategies share one separate attribute reading (anime, movie, suitability, and so on), which costs 2,944 tokens and 270 to 730 ms.

## Speed and cost

The numbers are from "tense but not bleak". They stayed nearly the same across the three requests.

| Strategy | Questions | Input tokens | Cost per 1,000 searches | Jev time | Qdrant time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A | 74 | 11,604 | $0.49 | 943 ms | 334 ms |
| B | 148 | 7,028 | $0.30 | 657 ms | 197 ms |
| C | 74 | 18,560 | $0.78 | 1,232 ms | 73 ms |
| D | 24–37 | 3,931–5,925 | $0.17–$0.25 | 690–1,047 ms | 219 ms |
| E | 3 | 4,973 | $0.21 | 297 ms | 164 ms |

Strategy B asks twice as many questions as A but costs 40% less and runs faster. Noul questions carry no level descriptions, and those descriptions are most of A's tokens.

## First look at the results

You judge the quality. These are only the things I noticed:

- **A, B, and D read the requests almost identically.** For "tense but not bleak", all three produce `tension` +1.9 and `bleakness` -1.9, and return the same top 5. If that holds on your requests, B or D gives A's quality at a lower cost.
- **B's results for "unreliable narrator" look the strongest:** Stay, The Machinist, Shutter Island, Anatomy of a Fall, The Prestige.
- **C is the only strategy that avoids the game shows** for "tense but not bleak". It returns survival thrillers: Open Water 2, The Requin, 247°F. For "unreliable narrator", its cosine ordering surfaces obscure titles. For the anime request, it can't express negations. It produced only `contemporary_realism`.
- **D can lose dimensions.** For "unreliable narrator", the group step skipped the emotional group, so `psychological` was never asked. The results drifted toward meta-narrative titles such as The Rehearsal and 8½.
- **E is the fastest at about 300 ms, but it's brittle.** For "unreliable narrator", it picked `narrative_structure` and then marked `ambiguity` as avoided. It returned PAW Patrol in the top 5.

One product note: the anime request surfaced an adult title in strategy D's top 5. The vote-count filter doesn't catch adult content, so a real search needs an adult-content filter.

## Page details

- Each strategy column shows its dimension weights as chips. **Show all attributes and dimensions** reveals every raw answer, and a hover shows the underlying values.
- Result cards keep the reason chips and the poster zoom. **Show scores** lists the stored score for each used dimension.
- The files are `app/server/prototype-jev-vector.server.ts` and `app/routes/prototype.jev-vector.tsx`. Both are new and uncommitted.

I checked the stored scores and the Qdrant ranks for those titles. There are three separate causes.

## 1. Jev can't see "sunglasses" in the 74 dimensions

No dimension means sunglasses, so Jev translated the request into `futuristic`, `visual_stylization`, `novelty`, `eccentricity`, low `contemporary_realism`, and low `historical`. That reading is a fair guess at "stylish science fiction", but it contains nothing that separates The Matrix from any other stylized science fiction title. The sunglasses exist only in the trope data: TV Tropes has tropes such as "Cool Shades" and "Sunglasses at Night". This request is a trope-shaped request, and the page currently runs without tropes.

## 2. Cosine distance pushes The Matrix out of the pool

Qdrant returns the 300 closest titles, and code ranks only those 300. The Matrix never enters that pool:

| Title | Weighted sum | Cosine rank | Sum of all 74 scores |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| The Matrix | 49.4 | 1,094 | 418 |
| Blade Runner | 46.7 | 914 | 375 |
| The Matrix Reloaded | 41.6 | 871 | 330 |
| The Matrix Revolutions | 39.2 | 1,653 | 319 |
| Blade | 30.7 | 3,454 | 320 |

The Matrix scores 10 on `futuristic`, 10 on `visual_stylization`, and 9 on `novelty`, which is a near-perfect match. However, cosine similarity divides by the length of the whole title vector. The Matrix is rich across many dimensions (a total of 418 across all 74), so its vector is long and its cosine is low. A short film like World of Tomorrow has high scores on the requested dimensions and little else, so it ranks first.

This is the same bias I saw earlier with obscure titles, and the pool of 300 doesn't fix it for well-rounded films. With a weighted sum of 49.4, The Matrix would land at about rank 20 if it were in the pool. The rank-20 sum is 49.5.

## 3. The weak weights act as tie-breakers against it

`eccentricity` +0.85 costs The Matrix ground, because it scores only 4 there. The titles at the top all score 8 to 10 on `eccentricity`. A dimension that Jev was only mildly sure about still moves the sum by 5 points, which is more than the gap between rank 1 and rank 20.

Blade is a different case. Its stored `futuristic` score is 4, which is reasonable for a vampire film. It fits "sunglasses" but not "scifi", so the fingerprint can't find it under this reading. Only trope evidence would.

## Ideas

- **Drop cosine for this query shape.** The query is a sparse weight vector, not a title profile, so cosine is the wrong metric. Two options:
  - **Payload range filters plus a Crate or in-code weighted sum.** Filter in Qdrant on the top one or two positive dimensions, for example `futuristic >= 7`, and scroll the matches without a vector. Then rank by weighted sum.
  - **A second named vector with dot-product distance.** This needs a re-index, but then Qdrant's order equals the weighted sum and the pool problem disappears.
- **Square or threshold the weights.** Use only weights above about 1.2 for ranking, or square them, so that mild guesses like `eccentricity` +0.85 stop deciding the top 20.
- **Add a popularity or quality prior as a tie-breaker.** Many titles tie near the maximum sum. Breaking ties by vote count or GoodWatch score would surface The Matrix over a 2015 short film.
- **Bring tropes back for the leftover words.** Code can detect request words that no dimension absorbed and run only those words through the trope name search. Here that means "sunglasses", because Jev's strongest dimensions all relate to "scifi". That keeps the trope query small and targeted, and it needs no extra Jev call.

Do you want me to add the filter-based retrieval and the weight threshold as extra options on the page, so you can compare them against the current cosine pool?

I agree with your ranking, and I measured it over 12 requests to check. The numbers support dropping E and C, and they point to A or B as the strategy to keep. Each request ran twice, with linear weights, a pool of 2,000, and tropes off, so the comparison isolates how each strategy reads the request.

## Measured over 12 requests

| Strategy | Same top 20 on a repeat run | Overlap of top 20 with A | Dimensions used | Negative dimensions | Jev time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A. Wanted level | 19.1 | - | 7.5 | 3.6 | 995 ms |
| B. Want and avoid | 17.7 | 12.4 | 13.2 | 9.1 | 545 ms |
| C. Ideal profile | 18.4 | 1.5 | 8.7 | 0 | 1,240 ms |
| D. Groups first | 19.2 | 17.9 | 7.1 | 3.3 | 1,044 ms |
| E. Pick three | 19.7 | 4.8 | 2.3 | 0.9 | 362 ms |

All values are means. The overlap and repeat columns count titles out of 20.

## What the numbers say

- **E: drop it.** Your observation holds. E uses 2.3 dimensions on average, and for 4 of the 12 requests it shares no title at all with A. It's stable only because it says so little.
- **C: drop it, and your instinct is right.** C never produced a negative dimension in 12 requests, by construction. An "ideal title" question can't say "avoid". For "not funny, not scifi, not fantasy, anime" and "political thriller without romance", its overlap with A is 0. It's also the slowest and most expensive strategy. Its one strength was avoiding the game shows for "tense but not bleak". That strength comes from cosine on a full profile, and you could get it a better way.
- **D: a cheaper copy of A, with a known failure.** D returns nearly the same results as A: 17.9 of 20 titles overlap. However, the group gate skipped dimensions that A used in 4 of the 12 requests. For "dark comedy about rich people", it missed `wholesome`, `hopefulness`, and `camp_and_irony`. For "clever dialogue, little action", it missed `adrenaline` and `violence`. D isn't faster either (1,044 ms against 995 ms), because it needs two round trips. It saves only tokens, about $0.20 per 1,000 searches. I wouldn't accept the misses for that saving.
- **A and B: the real choice.** They overlap on only 12.4 of 20 titles, so they're the only pair that differs in a meaningful way.
  - **A** is the most stable of the two and uses a focused set of about 7 dimensions.
  - **B** is almost twice as fast and costs 40% less, but it uses 13 dimensions, 9 of them negative. B over-generates avoids. For "scifi epic fights with huge battles" in your screenshot, B added `situational_comedy` -1.08, `sports` -0.92, `dialogue_centrality` -0.92, and `biographical` -0.82, although the request said none of that. B's lower repeat stability (17.7) comes from those marginal dimensions drifting in and out.

## My recommendation

Keep A and B, and drop C, D, and E. Then test one change to B before you choose between them: require a higher probability gap for negative dimensions than for positive ones, for example 0.8 for avoids against 0.4 for wants. If that removes the spurious avoids, B gives A's reading at half the latency, and I'd pick B. If it doesn't, pick A.

One caution about this validation: it measures agreement and stability, not whether the results are good. Two strategies can agree and both be wrong, as with the game shows for "tense but not bleak". Your judgment of the result lists remains the quality measure. The numbers only tell you which strategies differ enough to be worth judging.

The page now has eight columns: three A variants, three B variants, and a new approach C in two forms. The typecheck is clean, and I ran three requests through all columns with tropes off. I haven't opened the page in a browser.

## The columns

| Column | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| A1. Wanted level, linear | The earlier baseline: the 8 strongest weights above 0.6. |
| A2. Wanted level, strong only | The same reading, but only weights of 1.2 or more count. |
| A3. A2 plus genres | A required genre adds 0.3 to the normalized score, and an excluded genre subtracts 0.5. |
| B1. Want and avoid, symmetric | The earlier B. |
| B2. Want and avoid, strict avoids | A wanted dimension needs a weight of 0.8, and an avoided one needs 1.5. |
| B3. B2 plus genres | The same genre layer as A3. |
| C1. Kinds of title, cosine | New, described in the next section. |
| C2. Kinds of title, then A2 weights | New. The kinds select the pool, and A2's weights rank inside it. |

Each Jev reading now runs once per search, and every column derives its query from the shared readings. Differences between columns therefore come from the variant logic, not from run-to-run noise. The 23 genre questions ride along in the attribute request, so they add no Jev call. The weight shaping selector is gone, because the variants cover it.

## The new approach C: kinds of title

Two lessons led to this approach. First, Jev can't invent a realistic 74-number profile, which was the old C's weakness. Second, a sparse weight vector says nothing about what kind of title is wanted, which is how game shows win "tense but not bleak".

So the catalog supplies the profiles:

1. **Cluster once, offline.** About 20,000 popular titles are clustered into 48 kinds. The build takes a few seconds on the first search, and the result is cached in `node_modules/.cache`.
2. **Describe each kind in words.** A kind has its typical genres, its strongest and most distinctive qualities, and its unusually low qualities.
3. **Let Jev score the kinds.** One request with 48 Score questions asks how well each kind of title fits the request.
4. **Query with real profiles.** The centroids of the best kinds form the cosine query. Centroids are real full profiles, so cosine is the right metric for them.

The page shows the top kinds with their fit scores, so you can see what Jev chose.

## How I judge the results

- **The kinds reading is good.**
  - "tense but not bleak" selects a Thriller/Crime kind with tension and intrigue.
  - "dark comedy about rich people" selects a Comedy/Drama kind with satire, cringe humor, social commentary, and dark humor, at 3.74 of 4.
- **C2 is the best column on two of three requests.**
  - "dark comedy about rich people" returns Parasite, Swept Away, BEEF, and SKY Castle, which are about rich people. A and B return satire in general: Wonder Showzen, War, Inc.
  - "tense but not bleak" returns thrillers such as The Night Manager and The Taking of Pelham. C is the first approach that removes the game shows.
- **C1 alone is weak.** It finds the right kind of title, but it picks obscure ones, because nothing ranks inside the kind. The kinds work as a pool selector, not as a ranker.
- **B2 fixes B's problem.** For "scifi epic fights with huge battles", B1 used 14 dimensions with 7 negative ones. B2 uses 7 with none negative, and it now matches A2's results at 60% of the cost and about half the latency.
- **The genre layer acts, but it isn't clearly better.** For the science fiction request, it moved the list toward mecha anime, because those titles carry the Action, Science Fiction, and War genres together. It needs your eye.
- **The threshold (A2 against A1) changes little** on these requests.

## Costs

| Column | Input tokens | Cost per 1,000 searches | Jev time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A variants | 11,604 | $0.49 | about 940 ms |
| B variants | 7,028 | $0.30 | about 460–900 ms |
| C1 | 15,705 | $0.66 | about 590–1,200 ms |
| C2 | 27,309 | $1.15 | the slower of its two parallel readings |

C2 pairs the kinds with A2's reading today. Pairing the kinds with B2 would cost about $0.96 per 1,000 searches and should be faster. I'd try that pairing next if you like C2's results.

One issue remains visible: Parasite appears twice in C2's list. It's the catalog duplicate problem again, not a ranking bug.

Every search has the same three steps: Jev reads the request, Qdrant fetches a pool of titles, and code ranks the pool. The variants differ only in what they ask Jev and in how they use the answers. I use one running example: **"tense but not bleak"**.

## The shared request: attributes, genres, and request shape

Every column uses this one Jev request. Jev gets the request text, plus one question per attribute and per genre. Each question has three possible answers: required, excluded, or not mentioned.

- "Is *Anime* required, excluded, or not mentioned?" The answer is not mentioned.
- "Is the genre *Thriller* required, excluded, or not mentioned?" The answer is not mentioned, because the request doesn't name a genre.

Two extra yes/no questions ask about the shape of the request. For example: "Does the request name a concrete thing or trope?" The answer is 4%, so the trope search stays off.

A decided attribute becomes a hard Qdrant filter, such as `is_anime = true`.

## Reading A: "how much of this is wanted?"

Jev gets 74 questions, one per fingerprint dimension. Each question has five answer levels, from "avoid" (0) through "no preference" (2) to "central" (4).

- "How much *Tension* does the request ask for?" The answer is 3.9.
- "How much *Bleakness*?" The answer is 0.1.
- "How much *Romance*?" The answer is 2.0, which means no preference.

The weight is the answer minus 2. That gives Tension **+1.9**, Bleakness **-1.9**, and Romance **0**.

| Variant | Which weights it keeps | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | The 8 strongest weights with a size of 0.6 or more | Tension +1.9, Bleakness -1.9, Melancholy -0.8 |
| A2 | Only weights with a size of 1.2 or more | Tension +1.9, Bleakness -1.9 |
| A3 | The same weights as A2, plus the genre bonus | Same as A2 here, because no genre was decided |

## Reading B: "wanted? avoided?"

Jev gets 148 yes/no questions, two per dimension. They're cheaper than A's questions, because a yes/no question has no level descriptions.

- "Does the request ask for *Tension*?" The answer is 92%.
- "Does it ask to avoid *Tension*?" The answer is 2%.

The weight is twice the difference: 2 × (0.92 - 0.02) = **+1.8**.

| Variant | Which weights it keeps | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B1 | Every weight with a size of 0.8 or more | The earlier B |
| B2 | Wanted dimensions at +0.8 or more, avoided dimensions only at -1.5 or less | B invents avoids. For the science fiction request, it added *Sports* -0.9 on its own. |
| B3 | The same weights as B2, plus the genre bonus | |

## Reading C: "which kind of title fits?"

This step runs once, offline: code groups about 20,000 popular titles into 48 kinds by their fingerprints, and describes each kind in words. For example:

> Kind 12: mostly movies. Genres: Thriller, Drama, Crime, Action. Distinctive: Crime, Tension, Narrative Structure, Intrigue.

Jev gets all 48 descriptions and one question per kind: "How well does this kind of title fit the request?" Kind 12 gets 3.1 of 4, a war-drama kind gets 2.9, and a game-show kind scores low.

Code then averages the fingerprints of the best three kinds into one full 74-number profile. That profile is the Qdrant query.

| Variant | How it uses the kinds |
| --- | --- |
| C1 | Qdrant's closest 20 titles to the profile are the result. |
| C2 | Qdrant's closest 2,000 titles are the pool. A2's weights rank inside that pool. |

## The Qdrant query

Qdrant stores each title as 74 numbers, which are its fingerprint scores. A query is also 74 numbers, and Qdrant returns the titles that point in the most similar direction (cosine similarity).

- **A and B** send the weights and put zeros everywhere else: `[0, +1.9, 0, 0, …, -1.9, …]`. The pool is 2,000 titles. For the pool, Qdrant returns only the dimensions that carry a weight. The display fields are fetched afterward for the final 20 titles.
- **C** sends the full profile of the chosen kinds, for example `[0.05, 0.16, 0.03, …]`.

All variants use the same filter: a vote count of 2,000 or more, plus any decided attributes.

## The ranking in code

For A, B, and C2, code scores each title in the pool with a weighted sum: weight × stored score, added over the used dimensions.

> A title with Tension 9 and Bleakness 2 scores 1.9 × 9 - 1.9 × 2 = **13.3**.
> A title with Tension 9 and Bleakness 8 scores 1.9 × 9 - 1.9 × 8 = **1.9**.

Code then rescales the sums to a range of 0 to 1 within the pool, and adds the bonuses:

- **Genres (A3 and B3):** +0.3 for each required genre the title has, and -0.5 for each excluded genre.
- **Tropes, when the search is on:** up to +1 for the best matching trope. The trope search covers only the titles in the pool.

The top 20 titles become the result. C1 skips this step and keeps Qdrant's own order.

## Why C2 removes the game shows

In A and B, *Chopped* wins "tense but not bleak", because it has Tension 9 and Bleakness 0. Nothing else about the title counts. In C2, the pool comes from the thriller kinds, so *Chopped* is never in it. The Tension and Bleakness weights then pick the best titles among thrillers.

Our results are weak for this request because of missing knowledge, not because Jev misread it. That knowledge already exists in your data, in a field that the search never reads. I ran the diagnosis against the data and didn't change any code.

## What goes wrong for "super tense high octane car chases"

**1. Jev reads the request well.** It finds Adrenaline +2.0, Fast Pace +2.0, Tension +2.0, Spectacle +1.5, and the genres Action and Thriller. That's correct, and the language model's titles score well on these weights: 72 to 97, against about 101 at the top of our list.

**2. The fingerprint has no dimension for "car".** The 74 dimensions describe how a title feels, not what happens in it. On intensity alone, The Raid, Kill, and Extraction (hand-to-hand action) beat Bullitt (80) and Ronin (80). Every column fails the same way, because every column ranks on the same 74 numbers.

**3. The two sources of concrete content are too sparse.** I checked the language model's titles in the catalog:

| Source | Coverage of "car chase" among those titles |
| --- | --- |
| Tropes | "Car Chase" appears on 4 of 36 titles, and 10 of the 36 have no tropes at all. |
| TMDB keywords | 18 of 33 titles have a chase or car keyword. The vocabulary is fragmented: `chase`, `police chase`, `high-speed chase`, `car race`, `street race`, `getaway driver`. Only 1 popular movie carries the literal keyword `car chase`. |

**4. My trope query added noise.** It searched for all five words, and the name boost promoted junk: "super" matched Super-Soldier, Super-Reflexes, and Super Mode. The best matches, Car Fu and Cool Car, only came after those.

## The finding that matters

The knowledge that the language model used is already in your catalog. The fingerprint pipeline had a language model write `essence_text` and `essence_tags` for every title, and those fields contain exactly this kind of fact:

- **Bullitt:** "Iconic Car Chase", "a legendary, visceral car chase that set new standards".
- **Ronin:** "Iconic Car Chases", "particularly its legendary car chases".
- **Baby Driver:** "Electrifying Car Chases", "High Octane".
- **Death Proof:** "Stunt Driving Thriller", "built around thrilling car chases".

The prototype sends none of this to retrieval. As a quick test, I filtered popular movies to those whose essence tags mention "car chase" (47 movies, 0.7 s), and ranked them by A1's weights:

> Fast X, Retribution, Gone in Sixty Seconds, Baby Driver, The Transporter Refueled, Transporter 2, Bad Boys II, Collide, Lost Bullet 2, Lost Bullet, Transporter 3, Taxi 2, Getaway, The Transporter, Bullitt, To Live and Die in L.A., Ronin, The French Connection

Six of the top 20 are on the language model's list. Several of the others are good finds that the language model missed, such as Lost Bullet, Taxi, and Collide. This filter used only the tags, because `essence_text` has a full-text index and needs `match` instead of `ilike`. A proper full-text search over both fields should find more.

## How I'd solve it

The principle: Jev has no knowledge of the world, so every fact must come from your data. Jev's job is to route the request to the right data and to judge text against text, which your first prototype showed it does well.

1. **Add a third retrieval channel: full-text search over `essence_text` and `essence_tags`.** Your catalog has about 126,000 titles with essence text, against 72,000 with tropes. A language model that knows each title wrote the text, in the same kind of language that users type. This step needs no new data and no Jev call.
2. **Search only for the concrete part of the request.** Jev's dimension reading already absorbs "super tense high octane". The leftover, "car chases", goes to the text search. The per-word check from earlier does this split: "scifi" scored 98% absorbed and "sunglasses" 50%. I'd run the check on phrases, not on single words.
3. **Let the evidence filter, and let the fingerprint rank.** For a request that names a concrete thing, a title without evidence for that thing shouldn't win, however intense it is. Evidence from the essence text, keywords, and tropes selects the pool. A1 or B2 weights rank inside the pool. This is the same division of labor that made C2 work.
4. **Let Jev select among code-found tags.** Code collects the candidate tags and keywords that match "car chases". Jev then answers one yes/no question per candidate. It keeps `police chase`, `getaway driver`, and Car Fu, and it drops `foot chase`, `boat chase`, and Super-Soldier. This is one small request, and it removes the noise that a plain text match lets through.

## 2. Literal matching: "rich" doesn't find "wealthy"

Jev can't generate synonyms, but it can select them. This variation uses feedback from the first search:

- **D4c. Tag feedback.**
  1. Run D4's search.
  2. Count the most frequent essence tags among the top 50 matches.
  3. Ask Jev one yes/no question per tag: "Does this tag express what the request asks for?"
  4. Search again with the accepted tags as extra terms.

For car chases, I'd expect the accepted tags to include "Stunt Driving", "Street Racing", and "Getaway Driver". D4c costs one extra small Jev request, about 1,500 tokens and 300 ms, plus a second database query. It's the only variation here that makes searches noticeably more expensive. "scifi sunglasses" fails because no essence text mentions sunglasses. The fact exists only in the tropes ("Cool Shades", "Sunglasses at Night") and partly in the TMDB keywords.

**Verdict: skip it.** Two measurements decide this:

## Idea 2: cache by normalized request

**Verdict: build it. It's the largest saving available.**

- A Redis read of a stored reading takes 25 ms, and a write takes 23 ms. The webapp's cache utility already exists.

  - For "something to watch with my kids, no cartoons", the short criteria dropped "must be Kids" and "must be Intergenerational", but the results stayed the same.

## The new Crate column and analyzer

Your cluster runs Crate 5.10.9 with 12 shards per table. I checked the Crate documentation for what's possible. I didn't change anything in the database.

**What's wrong today**

- The text search runs over `essence_text` and `synopsis`. Both use the default analyzer, which has no stemming and no stopwords. That's why the prototype has to search "chase chases" by hand.
- `essence_tags` and `keywords` are plain text arrays without a full-text index. The tags hold the best evidence ("Iconic Car Chase"), but the search can't reach them. The keyword lookup only works on exact values.
- Trope names live in a separate table, so they need their own query and an ID join.
- A common word such as "dialogue" takes 0.5 to 1.0 s, partly because two fields with different weights are scored for many matches.

**What I'd build: one evidence column per title**

Add a column, for example `search_evidence`, that the sync flow fills with one text per title. The text would contain the following parts, in this order:

1. The essence tags
2. The essence text
3. The TMDB keywords
4. The trope names
5. The synopsis

- **Analyzer.** Crate has a built-in `english` analyzer with stemming and English stopwords. With it, "chases" matches "chase", "sunglasses" matches "sunglass", and words like "the" and "with" stop adding noise. The plural workaround and most of my stopword list would go away.
- **Weighting.** A single column can't weight its parts. I'd use two columns:
  - `search_evidence_strong` holds the tags, keywords, and trope names.
  - `search_evidence_text` holds the essence text and the synopsis.

  The query would weight the first column higher. That reproduces the "tag match beats text match" rule inside the index.
- **A custom analyzer instead of the built-in one.** Crate lets you define one with `CREATE ANALYZER`: a tokenizer plus filters such as `lowercase`, `stop`, and `stemmer`. The `stemmer` filter offers lighter variants such as `kstem`. A lighter stemmer merges fewer unrelated words than the default. I'd start with the built-in `english` analyzer and switch only if you see bad matches.

**What this would fix**

- Requests like "scifi sunglasses" would work in the first query, without the wider evidence fallback and its extra 0.5 to 0.8 s. The trope names would already be in the column.
- The plural handling, the keyword lookup, and the trope join would disappear from the search code.
- One `match` over two columns replaces up to four queries.

**What I couldn't verify**

- **Synonyms.** I found no synonym filter in the analyzer documentation that I checked. "rich" would still not find "wealthy". That gap needs a different answer, for example content tags written at fingerprint time.
- **Speed.** I can't say whether the new column would be faster for common words. The `match` itself dominates that time, and I'd have to measure it on a copy.

**How to roll it out**

- According to the documentation, `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` works on a table that has data. Only generated columns require an empty table. So this would be a normal column that the sync flow writes, not a generated one.
- The existing 126,000 titles need a one-time backfill. The inputs already sit in Crate, and the trope names need a join per title, so the job is a batch update in the sync flow. No model call is involved.
- I'd test it on a scratch table first. Copy about 5,000 popular titles, build both columns, and run the same eight requests against it. That gives you match quality and timing before you touch the production tables.
